stem: What does Garland's opening scene show about prairie farming?

stimulus.source_note: Hamlin Garland, 'Under the Lion's Paw,' Main-Travelled Roads (1891). Public domain. Text verified against Project Gutenberg (eBook #2809) and Original Sources.
stimulus.text:
Hamlin Garland, 'Under the Lion's Paw,' in Main-Travelled Roads (1891) (ellipses mark omissions):

"It was the last of autumn and first day of winter coming together. All day long the ploughmen on their prairie farms had moved to and fro in their wide level fields through the falling snow, which melted as it fell, wetting them to the skin all day, notwithstanding the frequent squalls of snow, the dripping, desolate clouds, and the muck of the furrows, black and tenacious as tar."

"'I didn't like the looks of the country, anyhow,' Haskins said. 'I was ust t' northern Ingyannie, where we have lots o' timber 'n' lots o' rain, 'n' I didn't like the looks o' that dry prairie.'"

options.text: It was easy work that left farmers with long idle winters
options.misconception: Background: Garland's ploughmen work all day in falling snow; there is no idle season in the scene.

options.text: It was mostly done by hired hands while owners lived in town
options.misconception: Background: the ploughmen in the scene are the farmers themselves, working their own fields.

options.text: It made farmers rich within a single season
options.misconception: Background: Haskins is driven out by grasshoppers and debt; Garland's farmers grow poorer, not richer.

options.text: It was grueling, wet, cold work done in mud and snow

rationales.A: Background: Garland's ploughmen work all day in falling snow. There is no idle season in the scene.
rationales.B: Background: the ploughmen in the scene are the farmers themselves, working their own fields.
rationales.C: Background: Haskins is driven out by grasshoppers and debt. Garland's farmers grow poorer, not richer.
rationales.D: Garland's ploughmen work all day in falling snow, 'wetting them to the skin,' in furrows of mud 'black and tenacious as tar.' The scene is toil, not ease.
rationales.general:
Picture a man behind a plough in late autumn, snow melting into his coat.
1. Read the weather. Falling snow, dripping clouds, cold mud rising on heavy boots.
2. Read the hours. All day long, moving to and fro across wide level fields.
3. Name the work. Grueling, wet, and cold, with no romance in it.
Remember: a writer who shows you the mud is telling you the truth the postcards leave out.
